1310.title: food as practice
1310.hook: the Gita sorts food into three kinds, and judges it by how you feel an hour later
1310.howItsDone: Hindus who draw on the Bhagavad Gita speak of food as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, after its chapter seventeen, and households draw their own customs from it, some avoiding onion and garlic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice was Charaka's way of eating: warm, unhurried, in a pleasant place, with the mind on the food.

Which foods are good? Ask that online and you'll get a list, then a different list, then an argument. The Bhagavad Gita answers a slightly different question. In its seventeenth chapter Krishna says, paraphrased, that even the food people love comes in three kinds, and he describes each one, not mainly by name, but by what the food does to the one who eats it, during the meal and after. Today, three kinds of food, and the hour after eating.
screen: `WHICH FOODS ARE GOOD?` → `THREE KINDS, IN THE GITA.` → `JUDGED BY WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: The three kinds follow the three gunas, the qualities the Gita sees running through all of nature: sattva, clarity; rajas, restlessness; tamas, heaviness. Sattvic food, paraphrased, increases life, vigor, strength, health, happiness and contentment: savory, smooth, nourishing, pleasing to the heart. Rajasic food is too bitter, too sour, too salty, too hot, too sharp, too dry, burning, and the verse says it brings pain, grief and sickness. Tamasic food is stale, tasteless, gone off, left over, unclean. Three things in how it sorts them. First, by effects. Sattvic food is defined by what it gives: life, strength, contentment. Rajasic food by what it leaves behind: pain and sickness. The test is the hour after. Second, the second list is full of too. Hot and sour aren't banned flavors; it's the excess that tips food into restlessness. That sits close to the Ayurvedic picture we've been following, where the same quality can settle or disturb depending on how much and when. Third, the verses describe qualities, not a fixed menu. Communities have drawn their own lists from them; some households, for instance, avoid onion and garlic, drawing on later teaching and custom. The verses themselves keep the focus on how food leaves a person. And they begin with the food each person loves, and sort even that into three kinds. Which turns the question around. Not only, what should I eat. Also, what does what I reach for tell me?
screen: `THREE KINDS, BY THE THREE GUNAS` · `LIFE, STRENGTH, HEALTH, JOY` · `TOO HOT, TOO SHARP, PAIN AFTER` · `STALE, TASTELESS, LEFT OVER`

segments.voice: Bring to mind what you ate most recently, and the hour after it: light and clear, restless and a little wired, or heavy and dull. There's no score; just notice, then come back to the breath and see what this moment feels like. If you pray, give thanks for food that left you well.

Your line: food as practice. The Gita's test is the hour after. See you tomorrow.

1311.title: food as practice
1311.hook: a knock at the door just as dinner is served: the Upanishad says to make much food for exactly this
1311.howItsDone: Hindu teaching treats feeding a guest as sacred, in the Upanishad's words, let the guest be a god to you; in some Hindu homes a first portion of the meal is set aside for a guest, a cow or birds before the family eats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice meant the Gita's three kinds of food, sorted by what they do to the eater, and the test of the hour after.

Dinner is on the table, exactly enough for the people sitting at it, counted out, served. And then a knock at the door. A cousin passing through, a neighbor, a friend of a friend who's hungry and a little embarrassed about the timing. Everyone at the table does the same quick arithmetic. The Taittiriya Upanishad, the same text where Bhrigu found food, has already thought about this knock, and its answer comes before the knock does. Today, food that doesn't stop at your own plate.
screen: `DINNER, COUNTED OUT.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `THE ANSWER COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Near the end of Bhrigu's story, the Upanishad gives this rule, paraphrased: do not turn away anyone who comes to your dwelling for shelter. And so, it says, gather much food, so there is food to give. That's the answer to the knock. Not a quick calculation at the door, but a kitchen that cooks, from the start, for more than the people already sitting down. Earlier, in its teaching to departing students, the same Upanishad says, in Sanskrit, atithi devo bhava: let the guest be a god to you. The guest isn't a disruption to the meal; the guest is honored at it like a god. The Bhagavad Gita says it from the other side. Krishna says, paraphrased, that good people who eat what remains after the offering are freed from their faults, but those who cook only for their own sake eat their own wrong. This lands in three places. First, it reframes these food days. Measure, attention, the hour after: all of that could stay private. These verses won't let it. Food as practice is also food as hospitality. Second, the order matters: offer first, eat what remains. In some Hindu homes a first portion is set aside before the family eats, for a guest, for a cow, for the birds. Third, it's practical. Make a little more. Keep a spare plate. The rule isn't a feeling about generosity; it's a way of cooking, decided before anyone knocks.
screen: `TURN NO ONE AWAY` · `LET THE GUEST BE A GOD TO YOU` · `COOKING ONLY FOR YOURSELF` · `A FIRST PORTION SET ASIDE`

segments.voice: Picture the place where you usually eat, add one more seat, and let a face come for it: a friend you haven't fed in a while, a neighbor, someone alone. Hold that face kindly with the breath, or if no one comes, hold the empty seat itself, open. If you pray, hold that person in prayer.
Food as practice. In the Upanishad: turn no one away, and make much food; let the guest be a god to you. Food that doesn't stop at your own plate. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. A kitchen that cooks for one more is ready for the knock. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1312.title: food as practice
1312.hook: a proud student is told to stop eating, and his father's lesson arrives as an ember
1312.howItsDone: Some Hindus fast on particular days as a devotional practice, while teachers of the Upanishads read Uddalaka's experiment as a lesson about the self, not as a fasting rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice and a knock at the door: make much food, and turn no one away.

A student comes home after years of study, sure of himself, full of verses. You met him back in year three, the proud one: Shvetaketu. His father, Uddalaka, decides to test him, and the test isn't a debate. It's a diet. Eat nothing for a while, the father says. Drink all the water you like. Then come back and recite what you know. The experiment sits in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. Today, what a meal has to do with a mind.
screen: `A STUDENT HOME, SURE OF HIMSELF.` → `THE TEST IS A DIET.` → `WHAT A MEAL HAS TO DO WITH A MIND.`

segments.voice: It starts with a claim, paraphrased. Food, once eaten, divides three ways. The coarsest part leaves the body. The middle part becomes flesh. The finest part becomes mind. Uddalaka puts it in one line, in Sanskrit annamayam hi somya manah: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Water, he adds, becomes breath, and heat becomes speech. Then the test. The text says fifteen days without food, with water allowed. Shvetaketu comes back, and his father asks for the verses. They don't come to me, sir, he says. So Uddalaka gives him a picture. A great fire has burned down to one ember, the size of a firefly. It can't burn much now. Add straw, and it blazes again. Go and eat. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and the verses are all there. And he understood, the text says. Three things. First, it's humbling. The young scholar who thought learning lived somewhere above the body finds it leaning on lunch. Second, it's kind to the body. Nobody is scolded for needing to eat; the plate is part of how a person thinks. Third, it's a doorway. In this same chapter Uddalaka will say tat tvam asi, that thou art. He's teaching his son what a self is, and food is one of the first things he reaches for. And plainly, since these days hold Ayurveda to a careful standard: this is a teaching story, not a fasting plan, and nobody should copy the experiment. What it offers is a way to see a meal: not fuel poured in while the real you is somewhere else, but an ember being fed.
screen: `FOOD DIVIDES THREE WAYS` · `THE MIND, MY DEAR, IS MADE OF FOOD` · `AN EMBER THE SIZE OF A FIREFLY` · `A TEACHING STORY, NOT A FASTING PLAN`

segments.voice: Rest a hand low on the belly if you like, and let a small ember come to mind, glowing, about the size of a firefly. With each breath in let it brighten a little, the way a coal brightens when air reaches it, and with each breath out let it settle and glow. If you pray, give thanks for the food that is holding you up right now.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya, the finest part of a meal becomes mind, and a hungry student's verses come back after he eats. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. The mind, my dear, is made of food. Rest well.

1313.title: food as practice
1313.hook: pure food, a clear mind, a steady memory, every knot loosened: one chain in the Chandogya
1313.howItsDone: Some Hindus cite the Chandogya's line aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih to explain care about what and how they eat, and Vedanta teachers following Shankara apply it to everything a person takes in through the senses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice and Uddalaka's ember: the mind, my dear, is made of food.

Pure food. A clear mind. A steady memory. Every knot loosened. That's a chain, link by link, and it sits at the close of the seventh chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. The chapter opens with the sage Narada admitting that, for all his learning, he's still in sorrow. It ends with this chain, and with a teacher showing him the far shore beyond darkness. Yesterday a hungry student got his memory back after a meal. Today the same Upanishad takes that thought much further, on the last of our food days.
screen: `PURE FOOD, CLEAR MIND.` → `STEADY MEMORY, KNOTS LOOSENED.` → `THE FAR SHORE BEYOND DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, paraphrased. When food is pure, the inner being is pure. When the inner being is pure, memory becomes steady. When memory is steady, all the knots are loosened. In Sanskrit it begins aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih. Ahara is what's taken in. Sattva is the inner being, the mind in its clearest sense. Notice three things. First, the direction. It runs from the plate inward: from something as plain as a meal toward something as large as freedom. Second, memory here isn't remembering where the keys are. Readers in the Vedanta tradition take it as a steady remembering of what matters, of who one really is. Third, the knots. The text doesn't name them. Readers have heard in them the tangles that bind a person: craving, confusion, old fears. Every one loosened, the line says. Then the scholar's turn. Shankara, the Vedanta teacher, reads ahara more widely than food: everything gathered in, what the eyes take in, what the ears take in, what the mind is fed all day. Pure intake, not just a pure plate. So the chain reaches a screen as easily as a kitchen. Now the look back. Bhrigu's vow. Eating in measure. A meal with the mind on it. The three kinds of food and the hour after. The guest at the door. The ember. And this chain. And wider, over the lens so far: the doshas, held as a way of noticing; the daily routine; the seasons met with care; and food, from the plate all the way to the knots.
screen: `PURE FOOD, PURE INNER BEING` · `STEADY MEMORY, KNOTS LOOSENED` · `AHARA: ALL THAT'S TAKEN IN` · `FROM THE PLATE TO THE KNOTS`

segments.voice: Go back through the day so far, not only meals: what the eyes took in, a screen, a street, a face, and what the ears took in, voices, music, news, letting each pass without grading it. Then find one knot somewhere, a tightness something left behind, and with each breath out let it loosen a little, if it will. If you pray, hold that knot in prayer.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya's chain, pure intake, a clear inner being, steady memory, and every knot loosened. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. Ahara is everything taken in, not just the plate. See you tomorrow.

1314.title: sleep
1314.hook: a stool stands on three legs; the Charaka Samhita says a life does too, and one of them is sleep
1314.howItsDone: In Ayurveda's classical routine, sleep at a regular hour belongs to the round of the day and night, and the texts count it among the three supports of life.

segments.voice: Last week ended with food as practice and the Chandogya's chain: pure intake, a clear inner being, every knot loosened.

A milking stool has three legs, and there's a reason. On a rough barn floor, three legs always find their footing. Pull one away, though, and the whole thing tips. The Charaka Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classical texts, describes a human life the same way, propped up by three supports. We've just spent our days on the first of them, food. The second is easily treated as empty space between the parts of the day that count. Today we start on sleep.
screen: `A STOOL ON THREE LEGS.` → `PULL ONE, IT TIPS.` → `THE SECOND SUPPORT.`

segments.voice: Charaka's word is upastambha, a support or prop, the kind that keeps something standing. He names three for life: food, sleep, and brahmacharya, which here means a disciplined, restrained way of living, especially around desire. Held well, he says, these three keep a body endowed with strength, good color and growth. Then, in a later chapter, a large claim about sleep. Paraphrased: happiness and unhappiness, strength and weakness, knowing and not knowing, even life itself, depend on sleep, on whether it's taken rightly or wrongly. That's a lot to hang on something done with the eyes closed. Three things follow. First, sleep isn't time off from the practice. It's one of the legs the practice stands on. A morning routine, a careful meal, a quiet sit: all of them lean on the night before. Second, happiness and knowing are on the list, so sleep reaches into the mind as well as the body. Third, rightly or wrongly. The text doesn't praise sleep as such. It speaks of sleep in the right measure and at the right time, and warns that too much, too little or the wrong hour does harm. And said plainly: the classical texts offer a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Sleep trouble that lasts, snoring that stops and starts, or exhaustion that won't lift: those go to a doctor. What Charaka adds to an ordinary evening is a change of rank. Sleep stops being leftover time, and becomes a support.
screen: `UPASTAMBHA: A SUPPORT` · `FOOD, SLEEP, A DISCIPLINED LIFE` · `HAPPINESS AND KNOWING HANG ON IT` · `RIGHT MEASURE, RIGHT TIME`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down and notice what's under you, a chair, a floor, a bed, letting your weight go into it a little more with each breath out: shoulders, arms, hands, back, legs, all the way to the heels. Nothing to fall asleep to; just the feeling of being held up by something that isn't you. If you pray, give thanks for the last night of rest you had.
Sleep. Nidra, in Sanskrit. For Charaka, one of three supports of life, with food and a disciplined way of living. Today's word.

1315.title: sleep
1315.hook: a bird tied to a peg flies every direction, then lands where it's tied
1315.howItsDone: Some Vedanta teachers read Uddalaka's lesson on sleep as a hint about the self, and the tethered bird is used in teaching to show the mind coming to rest in the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charaka's three supports of life: food, sleep, and a disciplined way of living.

A bird is tied to a peg by a long string. It takes off toward the trees, and the string pulls it up short. It tries the other way, toward the roof. Short again. It tries every direction there is. Finally, worn out, it comes down and settles right at the peg, the one place it was tied all along. That picture comes from Uddalaka, the father who taught his son with an ember. In the very next part of the Chandogya Upanishad, he turns to his son and says: learn from me about sleep.
screen: `A BIRD ON A STRING.` → `EVERY DIRECTION, PULLED SHORT.` → `IT SETTLES AT THE PEG.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka starts with a word. The Sanskrit for he sleeps is svapiti, and the text plays on it: svam apita, gone to his own. When a person sleeps, he says, paraphrased, he has gone home, united with sat, the Existent, being itself. That's why people say he sleeps: he has gone to his own. It's the Upanishad's own wordplay, a teacher's hook, not a dictionary entry. But look at what it does to the night. Sleep stops being a switch-off and becomes a homecoming. Then the bird. Tied to a peg, it flies in every direction, finds no resting place anywhere else, and settles where it's tied. In the same way, Uddalaka says, the mind flies in every direction, finds no resting place elsewhere, and settles down in the breath. For the mind, my dear, is tied to the breath. Three things in the picture. First, the day as flight. Messages, errands, worries, plans: the mind goes out and out, and it's meant to. The bird isn't scolded for flying. Second, the tether isn't a cage. It's what makes landing possible; without the peg, there'd be nowhere to come down. Third, the tether is close. Not a mountain, not a far temple. The breath, going the whole time under all the flying. Uddalaka is teaching his son what a self is, and sleep is one of his ways in. Every night, in his teaching, everyone takes the trip home, whether they notice or not.
screen: `SVAPITI: GONE TO HIS OWN` · `SLEEP AS A HOMECOMING` · `THE BIRD SETTLES AT ITS TETHER` · `THE MIND IS TIED TO THE BREATH`

segments.voice: Let the mind go wherever it likes for a while, tomorrow, yesterday, a conversation, a list, without chasing it back. Each time it tires of a thought, let it come down on one breath, the way the bird comes down at the peg, and then let it fly again if it wants. If you pray, rest in prayer at the landing.
Sleep. In the Chandogya, svapiti, played on as gone to his own: a nightly homecoming, with the mind settling in the breath like a tethered bird. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. The bird flies all day, and lands where it's tied. Until tomorrow.

1316.title: sleep
1316.hook: a king keeps asking what a person's light is, after the sun, the moon and the fire are gone
1316.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers read Yajnavalkya's teaching on the dream as a pointer to the self as the light of awareness, and study the waking, dreaming and deep-sleep states together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep as a homecoming: gone to his own, the mind settling in the breath like a bird at its peg.

What light does a person have? King Janaka puts that to the sage Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and the answers come one at a time. The sun, Yajnavalkya says: by its light a person sits, goes out, works and comes home. And when the sun has set? The moon. And when the moon has set too? Fire. And when the fire goes out? Speech: in the dark, a person goes toward a voice. And when speech goes quiet as well? Then, Yajnavalkya says, the self is his light. Today, the dream.
screen: `WHAT LIGHT DOES A PERSON HAVE?` → `SUN, MOON, FIRE, SPEECH.` → `AND WHEN ALL OF THEM ARE GONE?`

segments.voice: Why go there? Because Yajnavalkya is about to talk about dreaming, and dreaming is the proof. At night there's no sun, no lamp, no voice. And yet a whole world shows up: streets, faces, a house you've never lived in that is somehow your house. What's lighting it? The text's answer, paraphrased: in the dream, the person becomes his own light. The Sanskrit is svayam jyotih, self-lit. Then a passage worth hearing slowly. There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads, but he makes chariots, horses and roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, but he makes joys and pleasures. There are no ponds, no lotus pools, no rivers, but he makes ponds, lotus pools and rivers. For he is a maker. What is the passage after? First, the dream as evidence. Yajnavalkya isn't interested in what a dream means; this isn't a dream dictionary. He points at the fact that dreams happen at all, that something keeps seeing when every outer light is off. Second, the dreamer as maker. Every road in the dream was built that night, by the one asleep. Third, the turn back to waking. If something in a person can light a whole world in the dark, the same light is there at noon, quietly doing the seeing behind the eyes. That's where Yajnavalkya is steering his king. And one honest note: this is the Upanishad's teaching about the self, not a claim about how the brain dreams. It asks you to notice something, not to accept a theory.
screen: `NO SUN, NO LAMP, AND YET A WORLD` · `SVAYAM JYOTIH: SELF-LIT` · `NO CHARIOTS, BUT HE MAKES THEM` · `THE SAME LIGHT AT NOON`

segments.voice: Close the eyes and let whatever appears come and go, a color, a face, a room from this morning, without following any of it. Then turn gently toward whatever is seeing them; don't try to find it, just rest in the fact that the seeing hasn't stopped. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
Sleep. In the Brihadaranyaka, the dreamer becomes self-lit, svayam jyotih, and makes chariots, roads and rivers where there are none. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Even with every outer light off, something keeps seeing. Rest well.
